problem: It says the LIN break 'wakes slaves and marks a new frame'. A break field only delimits the frame. A sleeping LIN node is woken by a separate wake-up pulse (the bus held dominant for roughly 250 µs to 5 ms), not by a break field. A student who repeats this in an exam will lose marks.
fix: Write: 'The break is a long low pulse (at least 13 bit times) that marks the start of a new frame. A sleeping node is woken by a separate wake-up pulse, not by the break.'

problem: Calling CAN 'CSMA/CA' (collision avoidance) is not uniform. Many standard textbooks describe CAN as CSMA/CD with non-destructive bit-wise arbitration, and CAN does detect bit-level collisions during arbitration. A student may think no collision ever happens on CAN.
fix: Say: 'CAN uses CSMA/CD with bit-wise arbitration (some books call it CSMA/CA). A collision is detected bit by bit and the losing node stops without destroying the frame.'

problem: 'Standard bit rates are 125 kbit/s to 1 Mbit/s' reads as the full range of classic CAN. Classic CAN supports bit rates from about 10 kbit/s up to 1 Mbit/s; 125 kbit/s to 1 Mbit/s is only the usual automotive set.
fix: 'Classic CAN runs at up to 1 Mbit/s; automotive networks commonly use 125 kbit/s, 250 kbit/s, 500 kbit/s or 1 Mbit/s.'

problem: The list of errors that trigger an error frame leaves out the bit error, one of the five standard CAN error types (bit, stuff, CRC, form, ACK).
fix: 'A bit error, stuff error, CRC error, form error or ACK error makes a node send an error frame.'

problem: 'This gives predictable latency without a crystal in every slave' joins two different benefits of two different mechanisms. Predictable latency comes from the master's schedule table; not needing a crystal comes from the sync byte, which lets each slave calibrate its own oscillator.
fix: 'The schedule table gives predictable latency. The sync byte lets each slave measure the bit time, so slaves need no crystal.'
